video.title: From Nothing to $20k/month with Email Newsletters: Full Tutorial

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jazz, who runs Winnipeg Digest, a local events/community newsletter (about 35,000 email subscribers plus about 73,000 social followers) started in April 2024. Jazz explains audience growth via Facebook ads, annual exclusive sponsorships priced at about $12,000 per year, survey-based audience data, and a VA plus Claude/ChatGPT content workflow. He is now vertically integrating by selling Christmas light installation to newsletter readers, with plans for permanent lights and a fractional-CMO-for-equity model. The key takeaway is that a local newsletter is a cheap audience asset to build, sponsor sales are the hard part, and the audience can be monetised further through owned businesses.

ideas.name: Local city newsletter with annual exclusive sponsorships (Winnipeg Digest)
ideas.one_liner: A casual, events-focused local email newsletter plus Instagram account monetised by selling annual exclusive sponsor slots to local businesses.
ideas.business_model: Sponsorship/advertising: annual exclusive sponsor packages (one ad per newsletter), one-off ads, and Instagram posts
ideas.customer: Readers: mainly women aged 35-65 and homeowners in Winnipeg; payers: local businesses such as event venues, dentists, HVAC, plumbing and roofing
ideas.problem: Local businesses lack an engaged local advertising channel; residents lack a single positive source of local events and city updates
ideas.offer: Newsletter three times a week (events, community updates, bylaws, no crime or politics) plus Instagram, with one exclusive sponsor per category per year

pricing.model: Annual exclusive sponsorship, with higher one-off rates

price_points.unit: per year (12 newsletter ads, one per month)
price_points.label: Annual sponsorship (currency not clearly stated)

pricing.notes: Sell annual exclusivity rather than one-off sponsorships. Currency is not stated explicitly and the host speaks in USD. Jazz is in Canada, so CAD is possible.

acquisition_channels.details: About 90% of ad budget on Facebook ads; best ad is a 15-second video with local monument or drone footage and the text 'struggling to find things to do in [city]' plus '50+ events every week'. Spend about $3,000 a month for roughly 2,000 subs a month now, down from 4-5k a month early on.

quote.text: Usually have some sort of a local monument as the background. Video or image. Test both. I would say video has done better for me.
quote.speaker: Jazz

acquisition_channels.details: Instagram grown to about 73k followers with reels (restaurant reviews), now carousels; Instagram doubles as a sponsor lead source and a cold-outreach credibility tool.
Seasonal referral guides (top 50 things to do this winter, restaurant and hiking guides) drive shares and signups; giveaways and lead magnets being tested.
Sponsor leads come from inbound Instagram feature requests by young marketing coordinators, who then get sold on newsletter ads on a call; also relationships and outreach from the Instagram account.

ideas.delivery: Two VAs (one on events, one on writing) draft with Claude/ChatGPT; Jazz does a final review at night (about 1 hour). Sent via Beehiiv three times a week, 400-2600 words, fifth-grade reading level.
unit_economics_claims: Subscriber acquisition cost about 15 cents CAD early on, about $1.30 now
Subscriber worth about $8-9 a year if every ad slot sells
Newsletter revenue about $144k a year from annual sponsors
Time about 20 hrs/week now, about 7 hrs without sponsor chasing, up to 15 hrs/week once delegated
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated beyond ad spend of about $3,000 a month

acquisition.how: Facebook ads and Instagram carousels are largely automatable. Sponsor sales still need calls and relationships, which drag this down.

onboarding.how: A subscriber survey in Beehiiv is automated. Sponsor onboarding and ad drafts are manual but template-able.

delivery.how: Agents can draft the content. Events research, editing and final review currently need VAs and a human, though full automation is being explored.

billing.how: Annual invoices could be automated with standard tools. Jazz tracks sponsors in a semi-custom Notion CRM.

support.how: Little support is needed. Sponsor relationship management is mostly human.

uk_applicability.notes: Local newsletters work in UK towns and cities. The Beehiiv survey is fine under GDPR with consent. Use opt-in signups only. Pick a market without an existing local newsletter. The population of 100-150k+ rule of thumb transfers to UK towns and boroughs.

risks: Selling local businesses on newsletter advertising is hard
Sponsors can run out; revenue caps around $500k per year
Subscriber acquisition cost rises as the market saturates
Open rates can drop; aggressive list cleaning can remove real readers
Founder face association makes the asset harder to sell

ideas.name: Christmas lights leasing business marketed through the newsletter
ideas.one_liner: A seasonal, owner-operated Christmas light installation and leasing service sold to newsletter readers, with an upsell to permanent lights.
ideas.business_model: Per-job installation with annual lease/renewal; later upsell to permanent lights
ideas.customer: Winnipeg homeowners, mostly women who decide on home decor, reached via the newsletter
ideas.problem: Homeowners want Christmas lights installed without doing it themselves
ideas.offer: Design consult, installation and leasing of Christmas lights, with an early-booking discount

price_points.label: Initial anchor quote before items are removed

pricing.notes: Currency not stated explicitly. Permanent lights are about 4-5x the average order value of Christmas lights.

acquisition_channels.details: Ads and a giveaway in Winnipeg Digest to produce about 300 entries, then calls offering $150 off. Branded 'Lights' in the same colours as the newsletter. Five or six jobs sold before the season started.
Plan to add Facebook ads, with an expected lower conversion on colder leads.
Plan to offer a $100 steakhouse gift card for referrals.

ideas.delivery: Owner currently installs himself (3-4 hours per job) and plans to hire labour at about $15/hr, about three people for 3 hours, and later bring in an operator with equity.
unit_economics_claims: Cost per job about $200-300, lights only, excluding own labour
About 85% customer retention year over year
Targeting $100k revenue in year one, ideally $150-200k
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Five or six jobs sold before the main season started

acquisition.how: Newsletter promotion and Facebook ads can be automated. The design consult sales visit is in-person, which caps this.

onboarding.how: In-home design consults and mockups are done by a human.

delivery.how: Physical installation on ladders by people.

billing.how: Standard invoicing and payment tools can handle it.

support.how: Mid-season repairs and customer service are physical or human.

uk_applicability.notes: Christmas light installation is a real UK market. Needs public liability insurance, working at height safety and fitting UK electrical standards. Regional demand and pricing differ.

risks: Physical labour and safety at height
Quoting and close rate was poor early on
Cold leads from Facebook ads will convert worse than newsletter leads
Permanent lights are disliked by an experienced operator because of one-time sales and maintenance

ideas.name: Permanent lights upsell
ideas.one_liner: Pre-sell Christmas light customers on permanent gutter lights with a discount next year.
ideas.problem: Customers on the fence about Christmas lights may want a permanent solution
ideas.offer: Permanent lighting installed under gutters, with $500 off for existing Christmas light customers

acquisition_channels.details: Upsell to Christmas light customers during the season and from the newsletter.

acquisition.how: Upsell from existing customers and the newsletter.

uk_applicability.notes: Feasible in the UK with electrical and insurance compliance.

risks: A friend running home service businesses warns to avoid permanent lights because they are a one-time sale with maintenance headaches

quotes.text: stay away from permanent lighting. Stay away from jellyfish.

ideas.name: Fractional CMO for equity using the newsletter audience
ideas.one_liner: Winnipeg Digest acts as a marketing arm for local home service businesses in exchange for 15-20% equity.
ideas.problem: Local businesses struggle with marketing and customer acquisition
ideas.offer: Access to the newsletter, social channels and marketing handling in return for equity

pricing.notes: Considered unrealistic until the Christmas lights business proves the model.

acquisition_channels.details: Prove the model with Christmas lights, then approach other home service businesses.

ideas.delivery: Marketing run by Jazz and his team.

acquisition.how: Equity deals need personal trust and negotiation.

delivery.how: Ads and content can be tooled, but strategy is manual.

uk_applicability.notes: Equity-for-services deals are possible in the UK but need proper legal agreements.

risks: Local owners are unlikely to trust an equity offer without a proof case

quotes.text: we end up becoming like a fully fractional CMO type of situation where we they get access to Winnipeg Digest

ideas.name: Negative-CAC discount card or offers for newsletter signups
ideas.one_liner: Sell a local discount card or partner offers to new subscribers so the signup cost is recovered immediately.
ideas.business_model: Product sales to new subscribers (e.g. a $20 discount card) offsetting ad spend
ideas.offer: Discount card with 10% off at around 20 restaurants, sold in the signup flow

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook ads to the signup flow.

unit_economics_claims: If a subscriber costs $1 and one in ten buy a $20 card, ad spend is recovered

uk_applicability.notes: Works in the UK with opt-in consent.

quotes.text: buy this discount card for $20 and get 10% off these 20 restaurants or something, right?
quotes.speaker: Jazz

ideas.name: Spark Loop-style referral network for local newsletters
ideas.one_liner: A referral engine where subscribers see local business offers that pay per signup.
ideas.business_model: Selling leads to local businesses for each checked box
ideas.customer: Local businesses such as restaurants and auto repair shops
ideas.problem: Local newsletters cannot monetise through national referral networks
ideas.offer: Aggregate local business offers shown after newsletter signup

acquisition_channels.details: Partnerships with local businesses and newsletters.

quotes.text: I feel like someone needs to build a Spark Loop for local newsletters.
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Buying or sharing local business email lists to grow a newsletter
ideas.one_liner: Offer local businesses free ads or cash in exchange for sending their email list to your newsletter.
ideas.customer: Local businesses with unused email lists
ideas.problem: Businesses have dormant lists; newsletters need subscribers
ideas.offer: About $2,000 of ads for a 20,000 person list, or 10 cents per email

acquisition_channels.details: Partner with local businesses and segment the list into test groups.

onboarding.how: List verification and segmentation can be automated.

uk_applicability.notes: Adding people to a list without their consent breaches UK GDPR and PECR. Only usable as a partner-introduction email with a compliant opt-in.

quotes.text: I'll give you $2,000 worth of ads for your 20,000 person list.
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Niche or neighbourhood newsletters in large cities
ideas.one_liner: In big cities, niche down by demographic or neighbourhood, e.g. young dads in Austin or Williamsburg moms.
ideas.customer: Niche demographic audiences in large cities
ideas.problem: City-wide newsletters in huge cities are too broad

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook ads targeted at the niche.

uk_applicability.notes: Works for London boroughs and neighbourhoods.

quotes.text: Young Dads in Austin or something like that alone is probably like,000 people.
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Sell annual exclusive sponsorships
steps: Do not sell one-off sponsorships
Offer exclusivity by category (one HVAC company per year)
Price at about $12,000 for 12 monthly ads
Pitch it as a monopoly over the local audience

quote.text: you want to sell annual sponsorships on a exclusivity basis.
quote.speaker: Jazz

tactics.name: Sell sponsors on lifetime value
steps: Ask the business what a customer is worth
Compare to the ad spend, e.g. $5,000 customer vs $10,000 spend
Say you only need to find them four customers out of 35,000 readers
Target high-ticket or recurring categories like dentists, HVAC, plumbing, roofing

quote.text: I just need to get you four customers for you to double your um return on ad spend with us
quote.speaker: Jazz

tactics.name: Signup survey for audience data
steps: Send new subscribers straight to a short Beehiiv survey (8 questions)
Ask neighbourhood, home ownership, buying or selling plans, income
Use results like '75% homeowners' in sponsor pitches

tactics.name: Use Instagram inbound leads to sell newsletter ads
steps: Wait for marketing coordinators to ask for an Instagram feature
Jump on a call and sell the newsletter
Convert to annual ad dollars

tactics.name: Ramp publishing frequency
steps: Start weekly
Move to twice weekly then three times a week within a month when content overflows
Stop where content quality stays consistent

tactics.name: Short urgency-based subject lines
steps: Keep under five words and 40 characters
Include urgency such as 'this weekend'
Example: new Winnipeg Costco location

tactics.name: Facebook ad creative for newsletter signups
steps: 15-second video with local monument or drone footage
Headline: struggling to find things to do in [city]
Subline: [Newsletter] sends you 50+ events every week
Test video against image

tactics.name: Exclusive giveaway to build a leads list
steps: Run a giveaway of the product through the newsletter
Collect entries (about 300)
Call entrants offering $150 off for entering
Add a deadline discount

tactics.name: In-home design consult sales process
steps: Book a design consult
Sit with the customer, show before and after mockup
Walk through a booklet and anchor on a high price (e.g. $3,000)
Remove items down to about $1,500
Offer a time-limited discount if booked today

tactics.name: Pre-sell permanent lights during the Christmas season
steps: Offer $500 off permanent lights next year to Christmas light customers
Pull revenue forward from three years to two

warnings.warning: Don't clean your newsletter list automatically; tracking can show real readers as unopened and cleaning removes them.

quote.text: if you start cleaning your list you might start cleaning people that are actually reading your email.
quote.speaker: Jazz

warnings.warning: Don't try to close the sale at the first consult without a structured presentation; early quotes converted poorly.

quote.text: we sucked at sales for the first like seven, eight quotes that we gave out
quote.speaker: Jazz

warnings.warning: Avoid accepting casinos or clubs as advertisers if it conflicts with the audience vibe.

quote.text: Don't bring on casinos or clubs if that's not the vibe you're trying to set
quote.speaker: Jazz

warnings.warning: Markets under 100-150k are too small and over a million are too spread out for one newsletter.

quote.text: Anything under 100K is uh too small.
quote.speaker: Jazz

warnings.warning: Horizontal expansion lowers CPMs because national brands pay far less than local advertisers.

quote.text: your CPMs drop really drop a lot just because then you start having national brands
quote.speaker: Jazz

warnings.warning: Don't use ad networks like Beehiiv boosts for local newsletters; it harms reader experience and trust.

lessons.lesson: The audience is easy to build; the hard part is selling advertisers on a new advertising concept. Plan the sponsor sales process early.

quote.text: anyone can get to 10 to 15,000 subs. Anybody. It's just that acquiring sponsors for 10 to 15,000 subs.
quote.speaker: Jazz

lessons.lesson: First-mover advantage in an underserved local market lowers acquisition costs and creates a monopoly position.
Exclusivity and annual terms are the product; sell the monopoly over a local audience rather than impressions.
Own audience lets you vertically integrate and capture far more value than third-party ad networks; ad-only monetisation caps out.

quote.text: if you're going to just go sell ads on top of your local newsletter, it's going to be really hard to monetize.
quote.speaker: Jazz

lessons.lesson: Test a new vertical in a short, low-commitment window (10 weeks) so it can be dropped if it fails.
Learn the work by doing it yourself before outsourcing so you can manage labour properly.

quote.text: it's important that people get to know the weeds before they outsource
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: AI plus VAs can cut daily writing from about 8 hours to a small review step, letting the founder focus on sponsors.
Detach the founder's face from the brand if you want the business to be a sellable asset.
A time-compounding business where audience grows with the years is attractive because it is hard to lose.

quote.text: As long the longer I'm in the business, the more money I'm going to make.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Choose adjacent businesses that use your existing strength (marketing) and your audience's demographics (women making home decisions).

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with specific figures on sponsorship pricing, subscriber growth and costs, but the numbers are unverified and the Christmas lights projections are early and hypothetical. Sponsor revenue figures are internally inconsistent in places and currency is ambiguous (CAD vs USD).
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Host promotes GoHighLevel (sponsor read) and his paid TK Owners community; guest is active on Twitter and positions himself as a local newsletter advisor.
